title: Imamate of Oman
capsule: The Imamate of Oman (Arabic: الإمامة العُمانية) was an Ibadi Muslim theocratic state established in 1913 when Imam Salim ibn Rashid al-Kharusi led a rebellion against the Albusaidi Sultan of Muscat and his British-backed coastal authority, asserting the Ibadi principle that leadership must be elective and religiously grounded. The imamate controlled the Hajar mountain interior, including Nizwa and Ibri, rejecting both Muscat's dynastic claims and Britain's commercial presence in the region. Conflict was suspended rather than resolved by the Treaty of Seeb in 1920, which established a de facto partition between the elected interior imamate and the Muscat sultanate on the coast — an uneasy arrangement that held until the second imamate (1954–1959) was suppressed militarily with British support.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The 1913–1920 imamate's territorial extent in the Omani interior is broadly documented in British colonial records, though the precise boundary with the Muscat Sultanate was contested and the Treaty of Seeb left borders deliberately vague.
